title: Free expansion: why a gas never un-spreads
summary: Remove a partition and the gas rushes into the empty half; the molecules never all return by themselves.
alt: A box with a partition: forty molecules start in the left half; when the partition is removed they spread into both halves and stay spread out. Bars show how entropy rises.

steps.title: A gas in half a box
steps.text: A partition splits a box. All the molecules are in the **left half**; the right half is empty. This is a very **ordered** arrangement: only one way for every molecule to be on the left.

steps.title: Remove the partition
steps.text: Take the partition away. Nothing pushes the molecules: they just move at random. Within moments they have spread into the **whole box**. This is a **free expansion**: no work is done and the gas does not cool.

steps.title: Spread out and staying spread out
steps.text: The gas now fills both halves, about half the molecules on each side. There are **vastly more ways** to be spread out than to be bunched on one side, so that is where the random motion takes it.

steps.title: Will it ever go back?
steps.text: The molecules obey Newton's laws, which work just as well backwards. But for all {{N|0}} molecules to wander back into the left half at the same moment has a chance of only 1 in 2 for each one. For many molecules that is **never**.

steps.title: With only a few molecules...
steps.text: Try **N = 4**. With so few, all four are sometimes found in the left half again, by luck. The more molecules, the more impossible it becomes: the arrow of time comes from large numbers.

steps.title: Entropy
steps.text: Physicists measure this "spread-outness" by **entropy**. The unmixed state has low entropy; the spread state has the maximum. In a spontaneous change of an isolated system, entropy **never decreases**.

formulas.title: Entropy and number of arrangements
formulas.text: W is the number of ways the molecules can be arranged: more ways, more entropy.

formulas.title: Why it never un-spreads
formulas.tex: \text{chance all } N \text{ back in left half} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{N}
formulas.text: Each molecule is in the left half with probability 1/2.

challenges.prompt: After the partition is removed, the entropy of the gas:
challenges.hint: Is spread-out more ordered or less?
challenges.explain: The spread-out state has many more arrangements, so the entropy increases.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Why does the gas never move back into one half by itself?

options.label: The un-spread state is overwhelmingly unlikely

challenges.hint: Think of the number of arrangements.
challenges.explain: The laws of motion allow it, but the number of spread-out arrangements is so large that the un-spread one has almost no chance.

takeaways: A gas released into a vacuum **spreads out** and never returns by itself.
**Entropy** measures how spread out (disordered) the arrangement is; it is **S = k ln W**.
In a spontaneous change in an isolated system, **entropy never decreases**.

notes.title: Connects to
notes.text: This is an **irreversible** process: it is the picture behind the **second law**. Next: heat flowing from hot to cold increases the total entropy too.
